Having now gotten rid of these difficult questions about the origin of the world and about the beginning of the human race, the plan of the works requires addressing the problem of the fall of the first man, or rather, of the first men, and of the origin and propagation of death. God, in fact, had not created men in the same conditions as the angels, that is, in such a way that, if they sinned, they could not die. He created them in such a way that those who faithfully obeyed him, without death, would be followed by an angelic immortality and a happy eternity, and for the disobedient, death would be their just punishment and their most just condemnation. We have already noted this in the previous book [1].

But I believe that the nature of death should be delved deeper and more carefully. The human soul, although in reality it appears immortal, nevertheless also has a certain death, which is its own. It is called immortal precisely because, in a certain way, it never stops living and feeling, while the body is called mortal because it can be deprived of all life and by itself lacks it. The death of the soul takes place when God abandons it, like that of the body when God departs [2]. Then the death of both, that is, of the entire man, occurs when the soul, abandoned by God, abandons the body. So neither she lives from God nor does her body. This death of the total man is followed by the call for the divine Word's second death. «The Savior speaks of this when he says: Fear Him who has power to throw body and soul into hell. They could not suffer bodily death [13]. Who would not hurry to have their little ones baptized just so that they would not be separated from the body? [14]. In this way, faith would not be tested with the invisible reward, but it would not even be faith, because the reward for the work would be sought and collected instantly. In the new economy, however, by a more admirable and Savior grace, the punishment of sin has been transformed into an instrument of justice. Then it was said to the man: If you sin, you will die; and now it is said to the martyr: Die so as not to sin. Then it was said to them: If you transgress the commandment, you will die the death; and now it is said to them: If you refuse death, you will transgress the commandment. What then had to be feared in order not to sin, must now be accepted out of fear of sinning. Thus, through the ineffable mercy of God, the punishment of vices becomes an instrument of virtue and the torture of sin becomes the merit of the just. Then death was acquired by sinning and now righteousness is perfected by dying [15]. But this applies to the holy martyrs, to whom the persecutor put the choice: either desert the faith or suffer death, because the righteous love more to suffer than the first prevaricators suffered for not believing. Those, if they had not sinned, would not have died, and these, if they do not die, will still sin. Those died, because they sinned, and these do not sin, because they die. The guilt of the former brought the punishment, and the punishment of the latter prevents the guilt.

It is questioned, and not without reason, whether the first man, or the first men (since the marriage was two), before sin, were subject in this animal body to those affections, from which we will be free in the spiritual body once all sin has been purged and put an end to. If they were subject to them, how would they be happy in that celebrated place of beatitude, that is, in paradise? Who can call himself absolutely happy when he is affected by fear or pain? On the other hand, what could those men fear or grieve about, who were swimming in such an affluence of goods, in a state in which they did not fear death or any bodily illness, in a place where nothing was lacking to their good will and in which there was nothing that offended the flesh or the spirit of the man who lived in happiness? An imperturbable love for God reigned there, and the spouses lived among themselves in faithful and sincere familiarity, and from this love flowed great joy, without lacking an object of love worthy of enjoyment. They avoided sin without any concern, and in avoiding it no other evil broke out on them that distressed them. The measurements of its length, height and width are a symbol of the human body, in whose reality it came to men, as had been predicted. In fact, the length of the human body from the crown of the head to the feet is six times as much as the width from one side to the other, and ten times as much as the height, which is measured at the side or from the back to the belly. Thus, if you measure a man lying face down or face up, he is six times as long from head to toe as he is wide from right to left or left to right and ten times as tall as he is from the ground. Therefore the ark was made three hundred cubits long, fifty wide, and thirty high. Those who come to Him enter through it, because the sacraments emanated from it, with which believers and entities are initiated. Ordering it to be built of square timbers means the completely stable life of the saints, because the square, wherever you turn it, always remains firm. Let's go one step further and look at the development of the City of God through the descendants of Abraham. From the birth of Isaac until the sixtieth year of his life, in which his children were born, there is only one event worthy of mention. He asked God to give fertility to his wife, since she was barren, and the Lord granted his request, and when she conceived, the twins struggled while still in her womb. Distressed with this discomfort, she turned to the Lord, and received this answer: There are two nations in your womb, and from your womb two peoples will come forth. One people will subjugate another and the older will serve the younger. The apostle Saint Paul tries to glean from here a great testimony in favor of grace. And it is based on the fact that before being born, and without having done either good or evil, without good merits of any kind, the younger is chosen and the older is rejected, when in reality, with respect to original sin, both were equal, and, with respect to personal sin, both lacked it. Whoever thinks that such a promise was fulfilled in Solomon is in a great error. Notice only that: This man will build my house and that it was Solomon who built that magnificent temple, and not that: His house will be stable, and his kingdom will remain eternally before me. Pay attention, then, and contemplate the palace of Solomon, full of foreign women, who worship false gods, and the wise king himself seduced and precipitated by them at times into idolatry, and do not dare to think that the promise of God was mendacious or that he could not foresee what would become of Solomon and his house. However, even if we did not see those words fulfilled in Our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born of the lineage of David according to the flesh, we should not doubt it, lest we seek, vainly and inanely, another messiah, like the carnal Jews. After the death of Jesus Nave, God's people were governed by judges. In these years humiliation and work alternated with prosperity and solace, according to their sins and the mercy of God. At this time fables were invented about Triptolemus [ 39 ], who by order of Ceres was transported by winged serpents and carried, flying, wheat to the needy regions; about the Minotaur, the beast locked in the labyrinth, where, when men entered, they could no longer find the exit, prey to inextricable error. The fables of the centaurs, half horse and half man, were also faked; of Cerberus, a three-headed dog at the entrance to hell; of Phrixus and Heles, his sister, flying on a battering ram. The book of Hosea, the first of the twelve minor prophets, is headed like this: Words of the Lord spoken to Hosea in the time of Ozias, Joatan, Ahaz and Hezekiah, kings of Judah. Amos also writes that he prophesied in the time of King Uzziah. And he also adds Jeroboam, the king of Israel who lived at that time. Isaiah, son of Amos, whether from the prophet mentioned or from another non-prophet Amos—a more common sentiment—heads his book with those four kings cited by Hosea, and says that he prophesied in their time. Micah marks the time of his prophecy after Uzziah, and names three of the kings mentioned by Hosea: Joatan, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. These, as can be gathered from their writings, prophesied at the same time. To them must be added Jonah and Joel, of whom one prophesied under Ozias, and another, under Joatan, successor of Ozias. PROPHECIES OF JEREMIAH AND ZEPHONYAS ABBE CHRIST VOCATION OF THE GENTILES

1. Jeremiah is one of the major prophets, like Isaiah, not the minor ones, already alleged. When Josiah reigned in Jerusalem, and among the Romans, Anco Marcius, prophesied, the captivity of the Jews was already approaching. His prophecies lasted until the Third Month of the Captivity, as can be gathered from his writings. Next to him is Zephaniah, one of the minors, who says that he also prophesied in the time of Josiah, but does not say until when. Jeremiah, therefore, prophesied not only in the time of Ancus Marcius, but also in the time of Tarquinius Priscus, fifth king of the Romans, who was already on the throne at the time of the captivity. Jeremiah, then, says of Christ: The Christ, the Lord, the breath of our mouth, has been imprisoned for our sins, thus showing, in a few words, that Christ is our Lord and that he suffered for us. And in another passage: This is my God, and in his presence there is no one comparable to him. He found all the ways of wisdom and gave it to his servant Jacob and Israel, his beloved. Afterwards he was seen on the earth and spoke with men. Some attribute this testimony not to Jeremiah, but to an amanuensis of his named Baruch; but or-

After these three prophets, Haggai, Zechariah and Malachi, Ezra wrote at this same time when the people were delivered from Babylonian captivity. But he passes for more of a historian than a prophet. Her book is similar to that of Esther, in which her exploits are recounted, performed in praise of God not far from this time. Perhaps it can be said that Ezra prophesied Christ in the dispute that arose among some young people about who is the most powerful being in the world. And having said one that the kings, another that the wine and another that the women, who sometimes commanded the kings, the latter ended up proving that it is the truth that takes the cake. And it turns out that the Gospel tells us that Christ is the truth. From the restoration of the people until Aristobulus, the Jews were governed not by kings, but by princes. The calculation of that time is not enumerated in the canonical Scriptures, but in others; thus, in the books of the Maccabees [721, considered canonical by the Church and apocryphal by the Jews. preceded by our great theologian Moses, who announced the only true God and whose writings occupy the place of honor in the field of the canon. Thus, the Greeks, whose language has greatly enriched human letters, have no reason to boast of their wisdom as more ancient, and even less as superior to our religion, the only source of authentic wisdom. However - and this must be admitted - not only in Greece, but also in barbarian nations, such as Egypt, there was already before Moses the seed of doctrine, which for them was wisdom. If this were not true, the Holy Books would not say that Moses was versed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians, for where he was born and was adopted and nurtured by the daughter of Pharaoh, there he was educated in the liberal arts. But not even the wisdom of the Egyptians preceded that of the prophets, since Abraham was also a prophet. And what wisdom could there have been in Egypt before Isis, whom, after her death, was worshiped as a great goddess, taught them the letters? Now Isis was the daughter of Inachus, the first king of Argos, and at this time Abraham's grandsons had been born [74].

What is perverse or against order must necessarily be at peace in some, of some and with some part of the things in which it is or of which it consists. Otherwise, it would cease to be. Suppose a man is suspended by his feet, head down. The situation of the body and the order of the members is perverse, because the order required by nature is inverted, being above what should naturally be below. This disorder disturbs the peace of the body, and that is why it is annoying. But the soul is at peace with its body and strives for its health, and that is why there are those who feel the pain. And if, harassed by ailments, it were to separate, as long as the bond between the members subsists, there is some peace between them, and that is why someone has still been suspended. The earthly body does not stretch the earth, and by opposing its bondage it seeks the order of its peace and asks in a certain way, with the voice of its weight, the place of its rest [26]. And, once lifeless and senseless, it does not depart from its natural peace, whether preserving it or tending to it. If it is dammed -

But even though the dissolution of the corpse is prevented, its parts still unite a certain peace among themselves, and makes the whole body seek the earthly and convenient place and, therefore, peaceful. However, if it is not embalmed and left to its natural course, a combat of opposing vapors is established that offend our senses. It is the effect of putrefaction, until the elements of the world come together and its peace returns, piece by piece and little by little. The laws of the supreme Creator and Orderer, who governs the peace of the universe, are not exempt from these transformations. Because, although small animals are born from the corpses of larger and smaller animals, each corpuscle of them, by the law of the Creator, serves their small souls for their peace and conservation. And although some animals devour the dead bodies of others, they always find the same laws spread by all beings for the conservation of the species, pacifying each part with its convenient part, regardless of the place, the union or the transformations they have undergone [27].

And it is to show that, according to the definitions that Scipio uses in Cicero's books On the Republic, the Roman republic has never existed. In a few words he defines the republic, saying that it is the thing of the people. Solomon, the wisest king of Israel, who reigned in Jerus^, len, began in the following way the book entitled Ecle, siastes, included by the Jews in the canon of the Sacred^ Letters: Vanity of vanities, said Ecclesiastes, vanity of vanities and all vanity. What benefit does man get from all that work he does under the sun? And, linking to this idea the table of human miseries, he mentions the errors and tribulations of this life, and proves by the flight of time that there is nothing stable or solid here below. In the midst of this vanity of earthly things, he laments, above all, that since wisdom is superior to insipidity as light is to darkness and the wise man is as far-sighted as the fool is blind, everyone suffers the same fate in this life. With this he implies that evils are common to the good and the bad. And he adds that the good suffer as if they were bad and that the bad enjoy as if they were good. Here are his words: There is yet another vanity on earth: there are righteous people to whom evil comes like ungodly men and women, and wicked men who are treated as righteous men. The testimonies regarding the final judgment that I have proposed to adduce, taken from the Holy Scriptures, I will glean first in the New Testament and then in the Old. Although the Old precedes the New in time, the New precedes it in authority, because the former is nothing more than a prelude to the latter. We will begin, therefore, with the testimonies of the New Testament and, to give more strength to the proof, we will then add those of the Old. The Old Testament comprises the Law and the Prophets, and the New, the Gospel and the Epistles of the Apostles. This addition: And he set his seal, may mean that God does not want it to be known who belongs to the devil and who does not. It is absolutely hidden in this life, because it is uncertain whether he who seems to be standing will fall and whether he who seems to be already on the ground will rise. But by binding and imprisoning the devil, he is prevented from seducing the nations that belong to Christ, and which he previously seduced or held back. Because—as the Apostle says—God resolved before the creation of the world to deliver those souls from the kingdom of darkness and transfer them to the kingdom of the Son of his love. And what faithful person is unaware that the devil even now seduces the nations and takes them with him to eternal punishment? This is not done with those predestined to eternal life. There is no reason to worry that the devil frequently seduces those who, already regenerated in Christ, walk in the paths of the Lord. Because the Lord knows who are His, and of these, Satan does not seduce any by dragging them to eternal damnation. WHICH ARE THE DEAD PRESENTED BY THE SEA AND WHICH ARE THOSE DELIVERED BY DEATH AND HELL?

But who are the dead that the sea presented and that it had in its bosom? Because neither those who die in the sea escape hell, nor does the sea preserve their bodies, nor—what is most absurd—did the sea have the good and hell the bad. Who will believe this? Perhaps those who believe that in this passage the sea takes the place of the world are not led astray. The Apostle, in saying that those whom Christ will find alive will be judged with those who are to be resurrected, also calls dead, both the good, to whom he addresses these words: You are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God, and the evil, of whom it was said: Let the dead bury their dead. Furthermore, they can be called dead because their bodies are mortal. This is the reason for what the Apostle said: The body is dead because of sin, but the spirit lives by virtue of justification. Which proves that in a living and still corporeal man these two things exist: a dead body and a vital spirit. And yet, he does not say the mortal body, but the dead body, although a little later he calls them, as is more common, mortal bodies. The sea presented the dead that were in it, that is, the world presented the men that existed in it, because they had not yet died.

Let us now see what the apostle Saint Peter writes about the final judgment: In the last days there will come, he says, artificial impostors, who, carried away by their own passions, will say: Where is the promise of his coming? Because, since the death of our parents, all things continue as they were at the beginning of their creation. And they do not know, because they want to ignore it, that in the beginning the heaven and the earth were created, taken from the water and constituted in the midst of it by the word of God, and that is why the world of that time perished, drowned in the waters. But the heavens and the earth that now exist have been restored by that same word and are destined to fall prey to fire on the day of judgment and extermination of wicked men. 1. In the place mentioned, the Apostle does not speak of the resurrection of the dead. But in his first Epistle to those of Thessalonica he says: In regard to the deceased, we do not want, brothers, to leave you in your ignorance, so that you do not grieve in the way that other men who do not have that hope tend to do. CHAPTER ISAIAH
ON THE RESURRECTION OF THEM AND THE RETURN OF JUDGMENT

1. The prophet Isaiah says: The dead will rise, and those who were in the graves will rise, and all who are on the earth will rejoice, because your dew will give them health, but the land of the wicked will fall. The first thing refers to the resurrection of the blessed. And this another: But the land of the wicked will fall, it is well understood: However, the bodies of the wicked will fall into damnation. If we want to go deeper into what has been said about the resurrection of the good, these words must refer to the first: The dead will rise; and the second these others: And those who are in the tombs will rise again. And the saints that the Lord will find alive, if we ask about them, good things will be applied to them: And all who are on the earth will rejoice, because your dew will give them health. Health in this passage we can reasonably take for immortality. It is about the most perfect health, that which has no need for food or daily remedies. The prophet himself speaks of the day of judgment, after having spoken of hope to the good and terror to the evil. These are his words: This is what the Lord says: I will pour out on CAPUT.

HOW DO YOU UNDERSTAND THAT THAT THE SAINTS WILL COME OUT TO SEE THE SUPLEMENTS OF THE BAD PEOPLE? But how will the good come out to see the torments of the evil? Shall we say that they will physically abandon their happy abodes and head to the prisons to witness with the eyes of the body the torments of the wicked? God forbid we believe this! They will come out for knowledge or science. This word go out is indicating that those who will be tormented will be outside. That is why the Lord calls outer darkness those places opposite the entrance given to the good servant when he says: Enter into the joy of your Lord. Thus it will not be thought that the bad go in there to be known, but rather that the good seem to come out towards them through the science that allows them to know them, because they will know what is outside. The tormented will not know what happens inside, in the joy of the Lord; They will know what happens outside, in the outer darkness. 1. Many things are hinted at in the Psalms about the final judgment, but in general they are spoken of in passing and summarily. But I do not allow myself to pass in silence what is said very clearly about the end of the world. Lord, you created the earth in the beginning, and the heavens are the work of your hands. They will perish, but you will remain. They will age like a dress. You will change them like someone changes their cape and they will be transformed. But you are always the same and your years will have no end. As if the justice of the law ever attempted to provide punishment for the time spent in committing the offense! The laws, according to Cicero, establish eight types of punishment: fine, imprisonment, whipping, retaliation, ignominy, banishment, death and slavery. Which of these measures its duration by that of the crime, making the punishment last as long as the criminal act lasted, except perhaps the penalty of retaliation? [20]. This orders that each one suffer the evil that he caused to suffer. Hence that prescription of the Law: An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth. It is physically possible for justice to rip out the criminal's eye in as little time as it plucked it out of his victim. But if reason demands that a kiss given to another's wife be punished with a whip, is not he who did that in an instant whipped for a long time? And is not the sweetness of a short delight punished in this case with lasting pain? What will I say about prison? Should the prisoner remain imprisoned only as long as the act that earned him such a sentence lasted? In fact we see that it is very fair for a slave to be held hostage for many years simply for having verbally insulted his master or for having injured him with a blow, which passes in the blink of an eye. And fine, ignominy, banishment and slavery—punishments that are ordinarily irrevocable—are they not in some way similar to eternal punishments in relation to the brevity of this life? It does not occur to anyone to think that the torments of evildoers should be in direct proportion to the length of time that homicide, adultery, sacrilege and any other crime lasted, which should not be measured by the length of time, but by the greater or lesser quality of the sin. Can you imagine that the laws, when condemning someone to death, base the punishment on that brief moment that the execution lasts and not on separating him forever from human society? For what it means to separate men with the punishment of the first death from the mortal city, that means to separate them by death, the second from the immortal city. And as the laws of this city never return to society the man condemned to a capital sentence, so those of that city never return to eternal life the sinner condemned to the second death. How then, they ask, are these words of your Christ true: With what measure you measure, you will be measured, if a temporal sin is punished with eternal punishment? [21]. They do not realize that the measure spoken of here does not look at time, but at evil, and means: He who suffers evils, let him also suffer evils. Although perhaps one could understand the point that the Lord was speaking at that time, namely, about trials and condemnations. In this case, whoever judges and condemns unfairly, if he is judged and condemned fairly, receives the same measure, although not what he gave. He judged and is judged, but the punishment imposed on him is just, while the one he imposed was unjust.

An eternal punishment seems harsh and unfair to the human sense, because in the misery of this mortal life the sense of pure and elevated wisdom is lacking, which enables us to feel the enormity of the crime committed in the first prevarication. The more the man enjoyed God, the greater was his impiety in abandoning Him. And he who destroyed a good that could be eternal, became a creditor of an eternal good. Hence the condemnation of the entire mass of the human race [ 22 ], because the first guilty party was punished with all his posterity, which was in him as in his root. Thus, no one escapes that just and due punishment, if it is not for undue mercy and grace. And if all were transferred from darkness to light, the severity of the punishment would not appear in any of them. The context clarifies the meaning for us. Saint Paul was addressing the Gentiles who were already believers and said to them regarding the Jews who would later convert: Just as you in the past did not believe in God and have now obtained mercy because of their disbelief, so also these have not believed in your mercy in the present, so that they too may one day obtain it. Daily prayer, taught by the Lord—hence its Sunday name—erases the sins of each day when it is said daily: Forgive us our debts, and what follows is not only said, but put into practice: just as we forgive our debtors. The prayer is recited because sins are committed, not so that they are committed because it is recited. The Savior wanted to teach us with this prayer that, no matter how justly we live in the feverish night of this life, we will not lack sins for which we will need to pray and forgive those who offend us, so that God may forgive us. The Lord does not say: If you forgive men their sins, your Father will also forgive you your sins, so that, trusting in this prayer, we would surely commit crimes daily, whether by virtue of the authority that places us under the protection of men, or by cunning, deceiving men themselves. I would like us to learn not to think that we are without sin even though we are exempt from crimes. This is what God warned the priests of the old Law, commanding them to offer sacrifices first for their sins and then for those of the people. 1. It is indisputable that evil people do many things against the will of God. Therefore, when it is said that God changes his will, becoming angry—this is an example—against those who showed himself favorable, men change, not Him. The dispositions of the subject make us find God changed in a certain way. Something happens like when the sun changes for sick eyes and becomes soft, harsh, and delightful, annoying, while remaining identical in itself. The will of God is also called that which forms hearts docile to his commands. This is the meaning of the following words of the Apostle: God is the one who works in us to will. As the justice of God is called not only that which makes Him righteous in Himself, but also that which He produces in the man whom He justifies, so the law of God is also called the law of men, but given by Him. In fact, Jesus was addressing men when he said: In your law it is written. And in a psalm we read: The law of God is engraved on his heart. I am going to respond, lending God's mercy to my efforts, to the objections I have put into the mouths of my adversaries. I do not dare to affirm, but neither do I dare deny, that abortive fetuses that have lived in the mother's womb and have died there must be resurrected. However, I do not see why, if they are not excluded from the number of the dead, they should be excluded from the resurrection. Because one of two things: either not all the dead will be resurrected and there will be human souls that will remain eternally without bodies, like those who have lived in the womb; or, if all human souls will take, to resurrect, the bodies they have had, from whatever place they have left them, I find no reason to exclude from the resurrection children who have died in the womb. Whatever feelings everyone holds to what we said about infants already born, the same should apply to fetuses if they are resurrected [ 35 ].

[57] These happy expressions, which close with a flourish one of the greatest works that the centuries have seen, tell us something of much that could be said about eternal life, about eternal happiness. Augustine presents the theme from a merely human point of view, on the part of man, and that is why he encourages him with the hope of joy, love, praise and eternal rest in that love, in that praise and in that joy. There is a reason he wrote in the Enarration to Psalm 103 (3:17) that "the life of mortal life is the hope of immortal life." The citizens of the City of God must aspire to that goal, and whoever does not reach it has not known how to live the journey in their pilgrimage. These expressions: vacabimus, videbimus, amabimus et laudabimus, are those that fulfill the concern of the Augustinian man. United the portico of the Confessions: Et inquietum est cor nostrum doñee requiescat in te, with the epilogue of the City of God: Ibi vacabimus, et videbimus; videbimus, et amabimus; amabimus et laudabimus, we have solved the problem of today's "existential anguish" and Augustine's "eternal restlessness." Requiescere involves vision, love and praise. And this is the end of the City of God, and an end that will have no end.
